title: Southern Vortex above Blanco
caption: Star trails around the south celestial pole, Blanco 4-meter Telescope
celestial: Landscape photograph; the source does not name the site

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Stars swirl around the south celestial pole above the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in this timelapse image. Near the middle of the vortex sits Sigma Octantis, the southern hemisphere's pole star, which is fainter than Polaris, its better-known northern counterpart. Up and to the left of the telescope, the lit paths of two satellites cut across the star trails.

Photographers build timelapses like this by stacking many long-exposure images of the night sky. As Earth turns through the night, the stars appear to circle the celestial poles, the north one or the south one depending on the hemisphere.

The red squiggles in the foreground were made by someone walking with a red flashlight. Observatories commonly use red lights to protect night vision, because eyes that have adjusted to the dark are less sensitive to red light.

understand.summary: A timelapse made by combining long-exposure night photographs, credited to D. Munizaga. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as fixed points, and the trails appear only because the camera kept recording while Earth turned.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: The Blanco Telescope crowns Cerro Tololo, a summit in northern Chile that is home to NSF NOIRLab's Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO). The credit names the photographer as D. Munizaga.
alt: Star trails circling the south celestial pole above the Blanco telescope, crossed by two satellite paths, with red light squiggles in the foreground.
